title: “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY DOES PAUL SAY RUN INSTEAD OF “SEE HOW CLOSE YOU CAN GET”?
paragraphs: “FLEE SEXUAL IMMORALITY”: WHY DOES PAUL SAY RUN INSTEAD OF “SEE HOW CLOSE YOU CAN GET”?
Maybe the reason you keep losing the battle isn’t because temptation is stronger than you. Maybe it’s because you keep standing beside the fire God told you to run from.
There is a moment before almost every sexual fall when you still could have walked away.
Before “I would never do that” became “How did I get here?”
And for a few seconds, you were standing in front of it.
I know where my boundaries are.
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence of all:
How close can I get without actually sinning?
Then Paul enters the conversation with two words that destroy the entire strategy.
In the Greek text of 1 Corinthians 6:18:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — pheugete tēn porneian.
Not prove how spiritually mature you are by standing beside it.
Not see how close you can get.

The verb φεύγετε — pheugete carries the idea of fleeing, escaping, getting away. Paul does not portray sexual temptation as something believers should deliberately keep within arm’s reach so they can demonstrate their self-control.
He tells them to create distance.
And πορνεία — porneia, translated “sexual immorality,” was a broad Greek term for sexual activity outside the boundaries God established for sexual faithfulness.
Paul’s sentence is almost violently simple.
And maybe somebody reading this already knows exactly why.
You told yourself you were strong enough.
You told yourself you were only curious.
You told yourself nobody would know.
You told yourself it was only pornography.
But sin has always loved the word only.
Because “only” makes chains look small enough to wear.
Paul knew something about sexual sin that modern culture desperately wants us to forget.
Paul does not merely say, “Stop doing bad things.”
He says something breathtaking about the Christian body.
Your body is for the Lord.
The believer is united with Christ.
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore glorify God in your body.
Christian sexual holiness is not based on the idea that sex is dirty.
It is based on the truth that the body is sacred.
Sexual desire itself is not the enemy. God created humanity male and female. Scripture celebrates covenant marriage. Sexual intimacy within God's design is not something Christianity apologizes for.
The problem is not that human beings desire intimacy.
The problem begins when desire tries to become lord.
“All things are lawful for me”—but not all things are helpful.
“I will not be dominated by anything.”
The question is no longer merely:
Is this beginning to own me?
That is a terrifying question when asked honestly.
Because some people reading this know what it feels like to be owned by something they once thought they controlled.
Until pornography started deciding when you slept.
Until you began waiting for that person's message.
Until your spouse could no longer compete with the imaginary world inside your head.
Until deleting evidence became part of your daily routine.
And suddenly Paul's command does not sound prudish.
Run while your legs still remember freedom.
There is another biblical story that makes Paul's command almost impossible to read casually.
A young man far from home.
And Potiphar's wife repeatedly pressures him sexually.
Then one day she grabs his garment.
He does not stay to demonstrate his willpower.
He does not explain that they need healthier boundaries.
He does not remain in the room for another conversation.
Scripture says he left his garment in her hand and fled.
Joseph would rather lose his coat than lose his integrity.
Some of us keep trying to preserve the coat.
The friendship that stopped being innocent months ago.
The person who keeps awakening something you know should be buried.
We want purity without losing access.
We want freedom without closing doors.
We want God to deliver us from temptation while reserving the right to keep temptation's phone number.
Then we wonder why the battle never ends.
There are battles you win by standing.
But sexual immorality receives remarkably practical language:
Sometimes courage looks like standing your ground.
Sometimes courage looks like running as fast as obedience can carry you.
A person running out of a burning building is not weak because he refuses to prove how much smoke he can inhale.
And perhaps that is the picture somebody needs tonight.
You have been calling the flames “warmth.”
Maybe that is already the wrong question.
How much sin can I approach without crossing the line?
How closely can I walk with Jesus?
That changes the direction of the entire Christian life.
Because holiness is not merely backing away from hell.
And this is where Paul's argument becomes stunningly beautiful.
Immediately after commanding believers to flee sexual immorality, he asks:
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you...?”
Then comes the sentence shame desperately wants you to forget:
Not enough clean days on your calendar.
Not enough promises that you will never do it again.
And suddenly this passage is no longer merely about sexual behavior.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to improve your habits.
That means when Christ says, “Flee,” He is not a tyrant trying to steal pleasure.
He is the Savior who paid for your freedom warning you not to walk willingly back toward your chains.
But there is another person reading this.
Maybe ten minutes before opening this article.
And while reading these words, something inside you has been sinking.
Because you do not need anyone to explain conviction.
You remember the promise you made God.
You remember crying the last time.
“Jesus, I swear I'll never do it again.”
And now shame is preaching its own gospel to you.
God must be finished with you.
Conviction says, Come into the light.
The Gospel says something shame never wants sinners to hear:
Not imaginary sinners whose sins are socially acceptable.
Not polished church people who merely needed minor adjustments.
The person carrying memories they wish they could erase.
The person whose secret would shock everyone who knows them.
Paul knew the Corinthian church was not populated by people with spotless histories.
Earlier in this very chapter he names serious patterns of sin, including sexual immorality.
You were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
That may be one of the most beautiful sentences ever written to people with scandal in their past.
Your past can describe where Jesus found you without being allowed to dictate where Jesus is taking you.
Not because sin does not matter.
Not because God changed His definition of holiness.
But because Jesus Christ rewrites everything.
Repentance does not mean pretending the chapter never happened.
Grace means the chapter does not have to be the ending.
Maybe pornography has occupied years of your life.
Maybe you surrendered your body trying to feel loved.
Maybe somebody violated you and you have spent years confusing what was done to you with something that made you dirty.
What another person did against you does not make their sin your guilt.
Christ is not disgusted by the wounded person coming to Him for healing.
Maybe you have hidden sexual sin beneath Christian vocabulary, ministry activity, worship songs, Bible verses and Sunday smiles.
Then perhaps today is the day the hiding ends.
Because darkness cannot heal what it insists on hiding.
Where another person has been harmed, take responsibility rather than manipulating them with spiritual language.
Seek wise pastoral help and trustworthy accountability.
Tell somebody mature enough to help you walk in truth.
Do not merely pray for God to close a door while keeping your hand wrapped around the handle.
Because biblical purity is not ultimately the worship of self-control.
It is the worship of Jesus.
You are not trying to become clean enough for Christ to love you.
If you belong to Him, you fight because you have been loved at unimaginable cost.
The resurrection announces that sin and death do not get the final word.
The Holy Spirit means you do not fight alone.
And grace means failure does not have to become identity.
So perhaps you need to stop asking:
Perhaps tonight you need a different prayer.
“Jesus, how far do I need to run?”
Somebody else needs this message before tonight becomes another regret.
You do not have to fight alone.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to surrender tonight.
Not because temptation disappears after one emotional moment.

Because somewhere tonight, someone is standing at a door.
And perhaps God allowed these words to reach them before they touched the handle.
You do not need to find out what is waiting on the other side.
Not because Jesus is waiting behind you with condemnation.
Run because Jesus is ahead of you with freedom.
You do not have to see how close you can get to the darkness when the One who bought you with His blood is calling you back into the light.
